videos.title: A 300,000-Year History of Human Evolution - Robin May

questions.question: What is the main focus of the Gresham College lecture?
questions.ground_truth: The main focus is on human evolution and understanding it through the lens of evolutionary biology.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'The Gresham College lecture that you're listening to right now is giving you knowledge and insight from one of the world's leading academic experts.' (0:04-0:09)

questions.question: What is the primary factor that influences evolution according to the lecture?
questions.ground_truth: The primary factor that influences evolution is reproduction, specifically the impact on offspring's reproduction.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'So, um, so if I look around this hall, uh, for example, there are some people here who are going to be massively shaped by evolution because they're at the start of their potential reproductive journey.' (0:16-0:23)

questions.question: What is the leading cause of infant mortality under five according to the WHO data mentioned in the lecture?
questions.ground_truth: The leading cause of infant mortality under five is infectious diseases.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'And if you look at that data, first of all, foremost, I think it's important to say this is actually a tragic indictment of where we are today because many many many of these things are preventable um and should not be causing infant mortality, but they are because of inequality and poverty and all the other things that go with it. That notwithstanding in evolutionary terms, if we look at these leading causes of death, the majority of them are infectious diseases.' (0:36-0:44)

questions.question: How did the mating between Homo sapiens and Neanderthals impact modern human genomes?
questions.ground_truth: The mating between Homo sapiens and Neanderthals resulted in a blend of DNA, with some Neanderthal genes being retained due to their beneficial impact on survival and reproduction.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'When any two organisms mate and hopefully you might remember this from your school biology lessons. Um each of us carries two copies of each of our chromosomes. One inherited from our mom and one from our dad. When you produce sperm and eggs, those separate each sperm or egg getting one or the other. And then when you make somebody else, one of theirs comes together with one of yours and you get a new combination... And so what we see in modern human genomes is that roughly speaking, most of the chromosome, they're pretty random, except that it's pretty clear, I think, that here is a patch where we don't have any neandal DNA. Why is that? That must be the assumption is that's because whatever was on that chromosome from the was not helpful, was not good. um and has actually disadvantaged people carrying it in the sense that they have not reproduced as well as the rest of us and they have been lost from the population.' (0:52-1:03)

questions.question: What is the significance of the transition from hunter-gatherer nomadic humans to urbanized, agricultural humans?
questions.ground_truth: The transition to agriculture allowed humans to stay in one place, leading to urbanization, increased population densities, and the domestication of animals, which had profound impacts on human evolution.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'So, here's the first one. Um, this obviously is wheat. This is a crop that we eat. I said just now that one of the things that happened when we moved to agriculture is we diminish the diversity of our diet... And thirdly, um we started to live much more closely with other species, not quite like this, but with other species, by domesticating livestock, we started to share our homes, literally share our homes, uh, with all sorts of species, goats, dogs, sheep, cows, so on so forth, and a whole bunch of species that we didn't intend, but they came anyway, rats, mice, etc., etc. And that mixing pot has had a really profound impact on the subsequent evolution of humans over the last 10,000 years.' (1:24-1:34)

questions.question: How did the transition to agriculture impact the nutritional profile of early humans?
questions.ground_truth: The transition to agriculture led to a diminished nutritional profile as the diversity of the diet decreased, resulting in a reliance on a small subset of crops.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'The second impact is that it allowed humans to start to achieve densities, population sizes that we'd never seen previously. Prior to this point in human history, we were very small groups of nomadic hunter gatherers that traveled around. And you couldn't get very big because you couldn't stay in one place. You couldn't sustain a big population. Now you're staying in one place. You're growing your own food. you can expand agriculture, you can get to high densities. And high densities are very important for society. Um they're also quite important for some bad things, most notably infectious diseases. And thirdly, um we started to live much more closely with other species, not quite like this, but with other species, by domesticating livestock, we started to share our homes, literally share our homes, uh, with all sorts of species, goats, dogs, sheep, cows, so on so forth, and a whole bunch of species that we didn't intend, but they came anyway, rats, mice, etc., etc. And that mixing pot has had a really profound impact on the subsequent evolution of humans over the last 10,000 years. And let me show you a few examples of that. So, here's the first one. Um, this obviously is wheat. This is a crop that we eat. I said just now that one of the things that happened when we moved to agriculture is we diminish the diversity of our diet. Um, we had plenty more calories. That's a good start, but we missed out on things that were nutrients that were not necessarily present in all our plants.' (1:24-1:34)

questions.question: What is the significance of the lactase persistence gene in the context of human evolution?
questions.ground_truth: The lactase persistence gene allowed humans to digest milk as adults, which became beneficial when dairying was introduced, providing a significant survival advantage during times of food scarcity.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'And this is a very nice example of evolution, shaping evolution because, as you will know, um, those of you in particular who've got domestic pets, cats, dogs, etc. The basic rule for all mammals is that baby mammals drink milk and big mammals don't. Right? If you have a puppy, a puppy drinks milk. When you wean the puppy and have an adult dog, if you give your adult dog a bowl of milk, it will vomit it all back up again. Okay? And that is true for most mammals. It is also historically true for humans. Historically, evolutionarily, humans could also not consume milk as adults. We would drink milk as babies. we would wean and then we would become what's called lactose intolerant because you would miss the enzyme to digest it. That was not a problem until we started dairying. We started keeping cattle and sheep and other things for their milk. And then it became quite useful to be able to digest that milk even as an adult. There is a mutation that is presumably quite rare in nature that keeps that gene on into adulthood. And for the last million years or so, that's been totally irrelevant. But suddenly when we started to have a ready source of milk as adults, having that version of the gene was very beneficial. And the time it was particularly beneficial was when times got really tough. So for example, uh when in winter when there's no food around, um you were essentially on the brink of starvation. If you had a cow and you could drink that milk and not to vomit it back up again, you had a significant chance of survival. If you drank it and threw it back up again and got no calories from it, that was not helpful. And so what we see here is the very very strong selective pressure to have this version of the gene that allows us to metabolize milk.' (1:45-1:56)

questions.question: Can you explain more about how the lactase persistence gene works?
questions.ground_truth: The lactase persistence gene works by having a mutation that prevents the lactase enzyme from being turned off after weaning, allowing adults to digest lactose in milk.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'So, so how does the lactose gene work? So essentially you have a gene lactase which helps you digest milk sugars, lactose. If you can't digest the sugar, it makes you sick and you you vomit it back up again. So having that enzyme expressed produced is critical to be able to digest milk. Genes work. You have the thing that you're making. So that enzyme and what's called a promoter sequence beside it which tells the body when to when to put that protein into production, when to turn it off. So for instance, there are some proteins that are produced at different times of the menstrual cycle if you're female or when you go into adolescence or so on and so forth. You don't want you the gene for beards being turned on when you're six months old. Uh you only want it when you're when you're in puberty. Um and so so those promoters are if you like the timer lactase, this enzyme has a timer which says turn me off forever as soon as you finish you know wean as soon as you finish drinking milk from your mother. [snorts] Um, and that works brilliantly well in all animals, including ourselves. What we have done at some point in in in evolutionary time is there has been a mutation that has broken that switch and it stays on forever. [snorts] No use at all. In fact, in fact, possibly slightly disadvantageous because you're making a protein that's of no relevance. Um, up until the point when you start being exposed to milk as an adult, then massively massively important. So, so that's how it works.' (2:15-2:26)

questions.question: How does lactose intolerance affect the expression of the lactase gene over the life course?
questions.ground_truth: Lactose intolerance occurs when the lactase gene is not expressed due to a mutation that prevents the lactase enzyme from being produced, leading to an inability to digest lactose in milk.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'And the question about inheritance, so there are two sorts actually of lactose intolerance. I should have made that clear. The clean genetic type is that. So if you don't have the enzyme, you can't digest the sugar, you're lactose intolerant. There are secondary issues, for example, allergies to milk which are nothing to do with that enzyme um and and are to do with whether you've been stimulated by a particular antigen. So on so forth. So I guess the the cautionary tale here is don't be [snorts] listening to this at home and thinking, "Oh, actually my milk allergy is all nonsense. I don't have that gene. I'm going to go and drink milk." If you've been told you're milk allergic, don't drink milk. Okay? Regardless of whether you have this gene or not. There are different systems. Um, but yes, if you are genetically lactose intolerant, then whether your children are or not depends on the gene of your partner too because if you if your partner is lactose tolerant and they're lucky, they'll get that gene and not yours.' (2:35-2:46)

questions.question: How do mRNA vaccines affect our genome and long-term health?
questions.ground_truth: mRNA vaccines do not affect our genome or have any long-term health effects as they do not integrate into our DNA and are not inherited.
questions.evidence: The transcript fragment and timecode that support it is: 'So, mRNA vaccines, which we're all familiar with. So, the good so the clever thing about mRNA vaccines is they don't integrate into your genomes. They produce a protein, but they don't get inherited. So, [snorts] if like me and hopefully like all of you, you've been you've been vaccinated quite possibly with an MRA vaccine. You're not going to pass that on to your kids. It's not inherited in any way. Um, it is a transient, if you like, uh, process.' (3:05-3:16)
